description: A Computer Science student, pixel-art lover, and self-proclaimed final boss. I’ve always been fascinated by space and want to use the skills I have in coding, design, AI and creativity to get a little closer to the universe. For this challenge, I’m going solo as unknownY. :p
summary:
unknownY is a browser-based pixel-art educational game designed to help children aged 7–12 understand the challenges of living and working beyond Earth. Players choose between a Moon or Mars outpost and manage essential systems such as power, life support, food, communication, and radiation safety while completing a three-cycle training mission.

Instead of teaching through quizzes alone, the game lets players learn through exploration, resource management, environmental events, and the consequences of their decisions. Moon shadows, Martian dust, communication delays, ECLSS, greenhouse operations, and radiation shelter use are integrated directly into gameplay.

The project also uses NASA DONKI space-weather data to support a Solar Energetic Particle radiation training scenario. A Space Lab and collectible Space Notes provide deeper explanations of topics such as SEP events, lunar resources, Mars conditions, ISRU, and life-support systems.
details:
unknownY — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser-based educational pixel-art game created for children aged 7–12. The project turns the challenges of living beyond Earth into an interactive mission instead of presenting them only as facts or quizzes.

Players begin by choosing either the Moon or Mars. Each destination has different environmental conditions and mission challenges. The Moon introduces issues such as local shadow, solar power loss and radiation exposure, while Mars includes weaker solar charging, dust events and longer communication delays with Earth.

During each mission, the player controls a junior astronaut and explores a small outpost containing a Habitat, Solar Array, Greenhouse, Communication Station, Radiation Shelter and Space Lab. The player must keep five main mission conditions under control: Battery, Crew Health, Life Support, Food and Radiation Risk.

The systems are connected. For example, ECLSS uses electrical power to support breathable air, remove carbon dioxide and recover water. The greenhouse also needs water and energy to grow food. If food runs out, Crew Health gradually decreases instead of causing an instant failure. During radiation events, the player must recognize the danger and reach the Radiation Shelter before the risk becomes critical.

The game contains three mission cycles. Between cycles, players can spend Science points on upgrades such as Solar Efficiency, ECLSS Efficiency and Greenhouse Research. Progress is stored locally in the browser so Moon and Mars mission records, research levels and discovered knowledge can be retained.

NASA data is integrated through the NASA DONKI API. A server-side Vercel function securely requests Solar Energetic Particle data using a NASA API key. Historical NASA SEP data supports the radiation training scenario, while the game also attempts to retrieve recent space-weather information. A historical NASA training fallback is retained so the educational mission remains playable if the live API is temporarily unavailable.

Education is integrated in three ways. Players can press Learn near individual facilities to understand the system they are using. Space Notes act as collectible knowledge discovered during gameplay. A separate Space Lab allows players to explore additional topics such as solar flares, CMEs, SEP events, ECLSS, electrolysis, lunar water ice, permanently shadowed regions, regolith, Mars dust, communication delay, ISRU and mission safety.

The project was developed using TypeScript, Phaser, Webpack, HTML and CSS. GitHub is used for source control, while Vercel hosts the public web version and the NASA API proxy. Browser localStorage is used for lightweight progress saving.

The main creative goal was to teach space-system relationships through consequences and decision-making. Instead of asking a child only whether they know the correct answer, the game allows them to experience what happens when power is low, food production is delayed, communication is not immediate or radiation risk increases.

The project was designed around accessibility, short play sessions and clear cause-and-effect learning. Scientific concepts were simplified for younger players while keeping important real terms such as ECLSS, SEP, DONKI and ISRU. The intention is to make complex space exploration concepts feel understandable, interactive and memorable.
